Time Twist: Complete Japanese–English Translation Workbook

Evidence boundary: “Exact Japanese from ROM” is copied byte-for-byte at the decoded-text level from the authoritative extraction. “Probable normalized Japanese” is a conservative editorial aid. Kana left as kana is deliberately unresolved; inferred kanji were not present in the ROM. Control tags are program instructions, not punctuation.

Authoritative source: Time Twist Japanese-English script comparison.json (SHA-256 F98C7707659F72B484B7D7EC4F3DDF692522E5DD99DE62CCAE7AB107CA402AC5). Diagnostic review: none supplied; neutral diagnostics used. Exact/source order: japanese_exact is decoded from immutable Japanese banks; annotations are editorial aids

Method and field interpretation

All 2,052 records have a proposed final and patch-safe English field. Short simple lines may have identical literal and natural translations. Fixed-address natural meanings are expanded for analysis; their patch-safe forms retain the verified compact slot text. Every scenario patch passed the ROM character encoder and 24-column display validator. The materially revised banks passed native dictionary recompression: TT1A 1656/1669 bytes (13 free); TT1B 4022/4026 bytes (4 free); TT2 3834/3847 bytes (13 free); T22 1801/1812 bytes (11 free); TT3A 3733/3741 bytes (8 free); TT3B 1837/1840 bytes (3 free); TT4 4738/4741 bytes (3 free); TT5 3693/3702 bytes (9 free); T25 2363/2374 bytes (11 free); TT6A 2823/2833 bytes (10 free); TT6B 2298/2336 bytes (38 free); TT6C 3520/3536 bytes (16 free); TT6D 323/332 bytes (9 free). Unchanged banks retain the already-tested installed English maps.

The supplied diagnostic review was consulted for line-specific corrections, but its unsafe substring-based Japanese reconstruction was not copied. Speaker identity is derived from explicit labels, neighboring English speaker turns, and scene grouping. Ambiguity is recorded without leaving the line untranslated.

Scene summaries (17)

TT1A — 1995 prologue, fortune service, and personality test

On September 25, 1995, a newscast introduces physicist Dr. Simon's time-travel research. A televised fortune service collects the player's blood type, birth month, and yes/no personality answers, then predicts a meeting at a suburban museum. The narration establishes a polluted, anxious near-future Japan.

Translation choices: The personality-test prompts are Japanese declarative propositions answered yes/no. Natural English questions are used where that makes the interface clearer without changing the proposition.

TT1B — Devil Museum, possession, Dr. Simon, and the first time warp

The protagonist reaches the Devil Museum, meets a mysterious girl, and triggers exhibits tied to a sealed Devil. Comic flirting, a Nagoya/Owari-coded businessman, a church, and Dr. Simon's Time Belt lead into the first historical jump.

Translation choices: The protagonist normally labels himself おれ, but switches to gentler ぼく when protecting or reassuring the girl. The Devil's pompous voice and the businessman's clustered regional caricature are kept distinct.

TT2 — 1428 France: Pierre, Jeanne d'Arc, and the witch hunt

The protagonist arrives in 1428 France by possessing Pierre. He navigates a town, solves comic quizzes, meets Jeanne, and learns that the Bishop is exploiting a witch hunt under the Devil's influence.

Translation choices: Rough commoner speech, official/church formality, and stock elderly role-language are differentiated. Jeanne is 'Jeanne' in dialogue and 'Jeanne d'Arc' in historical narration.

T22 — France continuation: the prison, the pact, and the rescue

The Baron and jailer confront evidence of the Bishop's demonic pact. The protagonist works through the prison and execution grounds to save Jeanne and expose the Bishop.

Translation choices: The pact uses elevated, deliberately archaic diction; ordinary prison dialogue does not. Ecclesiastical titles remain titles rather than personal names.

TT3A — 1944 Germany: POW camp, resistance network, and escape

The protagonist becomes U.S. airman Cougar in a southern German POW camp. He escapes through a tunnel, encounters Simon and the Rebecca resistance network, and navigates Gestapo surveillance and coded clues.

Translation choices: Military ranks and Nazi terminology are translated plainly. The fragmented blue-note clue is layout-dependent and remains flagged for visual verification.

TT3B — 1944 Germany continuation: Schmidt, Hitler, and the border

Schmidt appears to capture Cougar and Simon but reveals himself as a resistance ally. Their flight toward Switzerland becomes a direct confrontation with Hitler under supernatural influence.

Translation choices: Simon remains formal and idealistic; Schmidt is terse and controlled. The script's caricature of Hitler is translated without embellishing or softening it.

TT4 — Ancient Athens and the Greek underworld

The protagonist appears as the physician Nicras in ancient Athens, revives a priest, receives Athena's plea, treats townspeople, and descends through mythological territory involving Hermes, Hades, Artemis, Poseidon, and Cerberus.

Translation choices: Greek names use established English forms. よみのくに is rendered contextually as the underworld rather than importing a Japanese Shinto cosmology into the Greek setting.

TT5 — September 1864 Atlanta: slavery, emancipation, and plantation life

The protagonist becomes George, a Black farmhand living with his mother Belle near Atlanta during the American Civil War. The chapter depicts racist violence, emancipation, plantation labor, Lincoln, and puzzles involving farm work and livestock.

Translation choices: The source's racist and dated material is translated directly, not sanitized. Enslaved characters' stylized Japanese speech is rendered as rural/working-class English without exaggerated minstrel dialect.

T25 — Civil War continuation: Meyer, Lincoln, and the river escape

The plantation storyline continues through Meyer's mansion, a meeting with Lincoln, armed guards, and an escape sequence involving George, Belle, a boat, and coyotes.

Translation choices: Meyer's self-serving politeness and Lincoln's measured formality are kept separate. Political claims are translated as character dialogue, not endorsed narration.

TT6A — Circa 4 BC Nazareth: Joseph, Mary, and Kashim the donkey

The protagonist becomes Joseph's donkey Kashim in Nazareth. Joseph struggles with Mary's pregnancy, the village debates prophecy and Roman rule, and a census order begins the journey to Bethlehem.

Translation choices: Biblical names use familiar English forms. Elderly じゃ/のう speech is treated as role-language, while the protagonist's donkey sounds and inner monologue retain the chapter's comedy.

TT6B — Journey to Bethlehem: desert trials, riddles, and animal comedy

Joseph, Mary, and Kashim cross barren country, seek food and water, solve direction and identity riddles, and meet talking animals before reaching Bethlehem.

Translation choices: Animal voices remain comic without becoming children's-book baby talk. Marked forms such as だっぺ are treated as characterization, not proof that the setting itself has a Japanese regional dialect.

TT6C — Nativity climax and final confrontation

At the Nativity, the Devil attempts revenge. The Magi, Joseph, Mary, Kashim, and the restored protagonist fight possession and work to save the infant Jesus before the story returns to 1995.

Translation choices: Caspar, Melchior, and Balthazar use dignified diction. The Devil's archaizing self-importance contrasts with the protagonist's blunt modern voice.

TT6D — Epilogue in 1995

The protagonist and the girl awaken in the present. She does not remember their shared history, but her fortune and the recurring incantation close the romantic and supernatural loops.

Translation choices: The girl's feminine sentence endings are conveyed through warmth and confidence, not a caricatured accent. The final growl remains deliberately ominous.

NOV2 — System menu and disk-change prompts

Start, wait, disk-side, insertion, and wrong-disk messages.

Translation choices: Uppercase is retained for system text; exact packed slots govern abbreviations.

NOV4 — Title-screen start prompt

The fixed start-menu label loaded with the title program.

Translation choices: Uppercase is retained.

TITLE — Title graphics

English wordmark and subtitle represented as graphics rather than scenario records.

Translation choices: The requested subtitle is retained exactly.

SON-KOUH — Kouhen direct-boot guard

Graphics text instructing the player to begin by loading Zenpen.

Translation choices: Natural English is expanded; the graphic itself remains a separate technical asset.

Control-code evidence

These functions are empirical summaries, not universal opcode names. Patch-safe text preserves the exact ordered tag sequence for every record.

⟦CTRL:0⟧Observed mainly as a dialogue-row or line advance. Exact runtime behavior depends on the surrounding script routine.
⟦CTRL:1⟧Observed as a stronger paragraph/page transition or staged reveal. Preserved without translating it.
⟦CTRL:2⟧Observed at page/box transitions and speaker-sequence breaks. Preserved without asserting a single universal meaning.

⟦CTRL:6⟧Observed as a major wait/page/scene beat. Exact behavior requires runtime tracing for each call site.

External cultural references
  • いわゆるひとつの: CiNii catalog record for 『いわゆるひとつの長嶋茂雄語録』, corroborating the phrase's cultural identification with Shigeo Nagashima.
  • ぼいん: Kotobank dictionary entry: slang for large female breasts; the cited historical example dates from 1968.
  • ぼいん etymology: Reference account connecting popularization to late-1960s television and host Kyosen Ohashi.
